Socrate n'a rien écrit ; on le connaît p: Socrates wrote nothing; we know him through Plato and Xenophon. “I know that I know nothing” is a later summary of the Apology: “I neither know nor think that I know”.
Platon : allégorie de la caverne, le mon: Plato: the allegory of the cave; the sensible world is only a shadow of the world of Ideas.
Aristote : logique, éthique de la vertu: Aristotle: logic, the ethics of virtue as the golden mean, observation of living things.
Stoïciens : distinguer ce qui dépend de: Stoics: distinguish what depends on us from what doesn't. Epicurus: pleasure as the absence of disturbance.
L'épicurisme n'est pas la débauche : Épi: Epicureanism is not debauchery: Epicurus advocated a frugal life.
Averroès, Thomas d'Aquin, Ockham, Machia: Averroes, Thomas Aquinas, Ockham, Machiavelli, Erasmus and Montaigne.
Averroès commente Aristote et défend l'a: Averroes comments on Aristotle and defends the harmony of reason and faith.
Thomas d'Aquin réconcilie Aristote et la: Thomas Aquinas reconciles Aristotle with Christian theology.
Rasoir d'Ockham : ne pas multiplier les: Ockham's razor: do not multiply entities beyond necessity.
Machiavel, Le Prince (1532) ; Montaigne,: Machiavelli, The Prince (1532); Montaigne, Essays (1580): “What do I know?”
Au Moyen Âge, les savants ne croyaient p: In the Middle Ages, scholars didn't believe the Earth was flat: its sphericity had been accepted since Antiquity.
Philosophes du Moyen Âge et de la Renais: Philosophers of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance
Descartes, Spinoza, Locke, Hume, Voltair: Descartes, Spinoza, Locke, Hume, Voltaire, Rousseau and Kant.
Descartes : « Je pense, donc je suis »,: Descartes: “I think, therefore I am”, methodical doubt.
Hume : on ne voit jamais la causalité, s: Hume: we never see causation, only habitual successions (the problem of induction).
Locke : l'esprit est une page blanche qu: Locke: the mind is a blank slate filled in by experience.
Kant : agir de façon que la maxime de so: Kant: act so that the maxim of your action could become a universal law. “Sapere aude!”
Rousseau n'a jamais écrit « l'homme naît: Rousseau never wrote “man is born good and society corrupts him” word for word: it's a summary.
Nietzsche, Russell, Popper, Kuhn, Sartre: Nietzsche, Russell, Popper, Kuhn, Sartre, Beauvoir and Arendt.
Nietzsche : « Dieu est mort », la critiq: Nietzsche: “God is dead”, the critique of values, the will to power.
Popper : une théorie est scientifique si: Popper: a theory is scientific if it is falsifiable. Kuhn: science advances through paradigm shifts.
Sartre : « l'existence précède l'essence: Sartre: “existence precedes essence”. Beauvoir: “One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman”.
Arendt : la « banalité du mal » à propos: Arendt: the “banality of evil”, about the Eichmann trial.
« Dieu est mort » n'est pas une célébrat: “God is dead” isn't a celebration for Nietzsche: it's the observation of a crisis of values.
Utilitarisme, Kant, vertus et dilemmes d: Utilitarianism, Kant, virtues and trolley dilemmas.
Utilitarisme (Bentham, Mill) : la bonne: Utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill): the right action maximizes total well-being.
Déontologie (Kant) : certaines actions s: Deontology (Kant): some actions are forbidden whatever the consequences.
Éthique des vertus (Aristote) : devenir: Virtue ethics (Aristotle): becoming someone courageous, just, temperate.
Dilemme du tramway : la plupart accepten: Trolley dilemma: most people accept diverting the trolley, few accept pushing someone, for the same outcome.
L'utilitarisme ne dit pas « la fin justi: Utilitarianism doesn't say “the end justifies the means”: it also counts the means among the consequences.
État, contrat social, séparation des pou: The state, the social contract, separation of powers and justice.
Hobbes : sans État, la vie serait « soli: Hobbes: without a state, life would be “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”; we hand our freedom to the Leviathan.
Locke : le pouvoir protège des droits na: Locke: power protects natural rights; a tyrannical power may be overthrown.
Montesquieu : séparer législatif, exécut: Montesquieu: separate the legislative, executive and judicial so that “power checks power”.
Rawls : choisir les règles sous un voile: Rawls: choose the rules behind a veil of ignorance, without knowing what place you'll have.
Montesquieu n'a pas inventé la séparatio: Montesquieu didn't invent the separation of powers out of nothing: he drew on Locke and on England.
Corps et esprit, conscience, test de Tur: Body and mind, consciousness, the Turing test and the Chinese room.
Dualisme (Descartes) : l'esprit et le co: Dualism (Descartes): mind and body are two substances. Materialism: the mind is what the brain does.
Test de Turing (1950) : une machine pens: Turing test (1950): does a machine think if it can't be told apart from a human in conversation?
Chambre chinoise (Searle, 1980) : manipu: Chinese room (Searle, 1980): manipulating symbols according to rules isn't enough to understand.
Le « problème difficile » de la conscien: The “hard problem” of consciousness (Chalmers): why is there something it feels like?
Réussir le test de Turing ne prouve pas: Passing the Turing test doesn't prove consciousness: that's Searle's whole point.
La chambre chinoise de Searle : tout mar: Searle's Chinese room: everything works, nothing is understood
Problème de l'induction (Hume) : rien ne: Problem of induction (Hume): nothing logically guarantees that the future will resemble the past.
Démarcation (Popper) : la réfutabilité d: Demarcation (Popper): falsifiability separates science from what isn't science.
Duhem-Quine : on ne teste jamais une hyp: Duhem-Quine: you never test a hypothesis alone, but together with a whole web of auxiliary hypotheses.
Crise de la reproductibilité : sur 100 é: Replication crisis: out of 100 psychology studies, barely more than a third were successfully replicated (2015).
Un résultat non reproduit n'est pas forc: A non-replicated result isn't necessarily fraud: often an effect that's too weak or a sample that's too small.
Open Science Collaboration : 100 études: Open Science Collaboration: 100 psychology studies replicated
Socrate n'a rien écrit. Maïeutique : fai: Socrates wrote nothing. Maieutics: helping minds give birth. Condemned in 399 BC.
Socrate n'a rien écrit. On le connaît pa: Socrates wrote nothing. We know him through his disciples Plato and Xenophon, and through Aristophanes' mockery in The Clouds. His method: question the other person until they discover they do not know what they thought they knew. He called himself a midwife of minds, as his mother Phaenarete was a midwife: that is maieutics.
La formule « je sais que je ne sais rien: The phrase "I know that I know nothing" sums up Plato's Apology after the fact, where Socrates says more modestly: "I do not know, and I do not think I know". That is already an advantage over those who think they know. In 399 BC Athens condemned him for impiety and corrupting the young; he drank the hemlock rather than flee.
La caverne et le juste milieu: The cave and the golden mean
Platon : la caverne, le monde des Idées,: Plato: the cave, the world of Ideas, the Academy. Aristotle: logic, the mean, the Lyceum.
Dans la République, livre VII, Platon im: In the Republic, book VII, Plato imagines prisoners chained at the back of a cave, who take the shadows cast on the wall for reality. One of them, freed, discovers the objects, then the sun. For Plato the world we perceive is only a shadow of the world of Ideas, which reason alone can reach. He founded the Academy in Athens.
Son élève Aristote revient sur terre : i: His pupil Aristotle came back down to earth: he observed living things, classified, and formalised logic with the syllogism: "all men are mortal, Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is mortal". For him virtue is a mean: courage lies between cowardice and recklessness. Around 343 BC Philip II of Macedon hired him as tutor to his son, the future Alexander. He then founded the Lyceum.
Stoïciens : distinguer ce qui dépend de: Stoics: tell apart what is up to us. Epicurus: pleasure as absence of trouble, a frugal life.
Les stoïciens tirent leur nom du Portiqu: The Stoics take their name from the Painted Porch of Athens, the stoa, where Zeno of Citium taught around 300 BC. The Enchiridion of Epictetus, compiled by his disciple Arrian, opens with their central idea: of things, some depend on us, others do not. Our judgements depend on us; the weather, health, other people's opinions do not. Peace comes from not tormenting yourself over the second category.
Épicure, au Jardin, place le bonheur dan: Epicurus, in the Garden, placed happiness in pleasure, but understood as the absence of trouble, ataraxia. He made do with bread, water and a little cheese: the "epicurean" fond of orgies is a caricature. As for Diogenes of Sinope, he did not live in a barrel but in a large earthenware jar, a pithos.
Averroès : « le Commentateur » d'Aristot: Averroes: Aristotle's "Commentator". Aquinas: Aristotle in the service of theology, double effect.
Au XIIe siècle, à Cordoue, Ibn Rushd, qu: In the 12th century, in Córdoba, Ibn Rushd, whom the Latins called Averroes, commented on Aristotle's work so carefully that he was nicknamed simply "the Commentator". He defended the agreement of reason and faith. His commentaries passed Aristotle on to Latin Europe.
Au siècle suivant, Thomas d'Aquin fait d: In the following century Thomas Aquinas made Aristotle an ally of Christian theology in his Summa Theologica, written from 1266 to 1273. The principle of double effect is attributed to him: an action aimed at a good may be permitted even if it brings about a foreseen but unintended harm. It is still used in medicine, when relieving pain risks shortening life.
Rasoir d'Ockham : l'explication la plus: Ockham's razor: the most economical explanation first. Universals: realists versus nominalists. A round Earth in the Middle Ages.
Le rasoir d'Ockham conseille, entre deux: Ockham's razor advises preferring, between two explanations, the more economical: do not multiply entities beyond necessity. The exact phrase does not appear as such in William of Ockham, a 14th-century English Franciscan, but the idea is his. It has become a scientific reflex: the simplest hypothesis first.
Ockham est aussi un champion de la quere: Ockham was also a champion in the dispute over universals. Does "the horse" exist somewhere, in addition to particular horses? Realists say yes; nominalists, Ockham among them, answer that it is only a convenient name. And no, medieval scholars did not think the Earth was flat: Bede or Sacrobosco knew it was round. That myth dates mainly from the 19th century.
Le Prince et Que sais-je ?: The Prince and What do I know?
Machiavel : Le Prince, écrit en 1513, pu: Machiavelli: The Prince, written 1513, published 1532. Montaigne: the Essays (1580), "What do I know?".
Machiavel écrit Le Prince en 1513 ; il n: Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513; it only came out in 1532, five years after his death. He describes power as it is exercised, not as it should be: a prince must sometimes know how to do wrong. The phrase "the end justifies the means" does not appear as such. At the same time Erasmus published In Praise of Folly (1511) and Thomas More coined the word Utopia (1516), from the Greek for "nowhere".
Montaigne publie en 1580, à Bordeaux, la: Montaigne published the first edition of the Essays in 1580, in Bordeaux, and kept adding to them until his death in 1592. His motto, "What do I know?", was engraved in 1576 on a medal with a pair of scales: weigh, doubt, take oneself as the subject of study. His friend La Boétie had written the Discourse on Voluntary Servitude: "Resolve to serve no more, and you are free."
Doute méthodique → « Je pense, donc je s: Methodical doubt → "I think, therefore I am" (1637). Cartesian coordinates. Pascal's wager (1670).
Descartes décide de rejeter tout ce dont: Descartes decides to reject everything that can be doubted: the senses that deceive, dreams that resemble waking life, and even mathematics, in case an evil demon is deceiving him. One thing alone resists: while he doubts, he thinks, so he exists. "I think, therefore I am" appears in French in the Discourse on Method in 1637; the Latin "cogito, ergo sum" comes from the Principles, in 1644.
La même année 1637, dans La Géométrie, i: That same year, 1637, in La Géométrie, he linked algebra and geometry through coordinates: the "Cartesian" frame is named after him. His contemporary Pascal proposed a wager: believing in God costs little if you are wrong and gains infinitely if you are right, an expected-value argument published in the Pensées in 1670.
Locke (1690) : l'esprit, page blanche. H: Locke (1690): the mind as a blank page. Hume: we do not see causation; induction is not a proof.
En face, les empiristes anglais. Pour Jo: Facing them, the British empiricists. For John Locke, in the Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690), the mind at birth is a blank page: all our ideas come from experience. No innate ideas.
David Hume pousse plus loin. On ne voit: David Hume went further. We never see the cause itself, only one thing that usually follows another. The sun has always risen, but nothing logically guarantees it will rise tomorrow: that is the problem of induction. We generalise out of habit, not proof. Kant would say that Hume woke him from his "dogmatic slumber".
Kant (1784) : « Sapere aude ! ». Encyclo: Kant (1784): "Sapere aude!". Encyclopédie: 17 volumes of text. "Voltaire's" line is Evelyn Hall's (1906).
En 1784, dans « Qu'est-ce que les Lumièr: In 1784, in "What is Enlightenment?", Kant gave the age its motto: "Sapere aude!", dare to use your own understanding. Enlightenment means leaving the tutelage in which one keeps oneself. The philosopher of Königsberg was thought so regular that, according to legend, his neighbours set their watches by his walk.
En France, Diderot et d'Alembert dirigen: In France Diderot and d'Alembert edited the Encyclopédie: 17 volumes of text from 1751 to 1765, plus 11 of plates. Rousseau, in The Social Contract (1762), wanted law to express the general will. And the line "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it" is not Voltaire's: it is Evelyn Beatrice Hall's, summing up his thought in 1906.
« Dieu est mort » (Le Gai Savoir, 1882): "God is dead" (The Gay Science, 1882): a diagnosis, not a celebration. Nietzsche was not an antisemite.
« Dieu est mort » apparaît dans Le Gai S: "God is dead" appears in The Gay Science in 1882, notably in the scene of the madman who announces it in the marketplace. It is not a victory cry: it is an anxious diagnosis. If the West no longer believes in God, on what can it ground its values? Nietzsche calls for all of them to be re-evaluated.
On l'a récupéré à contresens. Nietzsche: He has been hijacked against his meaning. Nietzsche despised antisemitism and German nationalism. His sister Elisabeth, married to an antisemite, falsified his manuscripts after his death to make him a thinker for the regime she admired.
Popper (1934) : scientifique = réfutable: Popper (1934): scientific = refutable. Kuhn (1962): science advances by paradigm shifts.
En 1934, à Vienne, Karl Popper publie Lo: In 1934, in Vienna, Karl Popper published Logik der Forschung. For him a theory is scientific if it can be refuted by an observation. A thousand white swans do not prove that all swans are white; a single black swan proves the opposite. A theory that explains everything, whatever happens, explains nothing.
En 1962, Thomas Kuhn décrit autre chose: In 1962 Thomas Kuhn described something else in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions: normal science works within a shared framework, a paradigm, and does not abandon it at the first anomaly. When anomalies pile up, a revolution replaces the whole framework, like Copernicus replacing Ptolemy.
Sartre: existence precedes essence. Beauvoir: one becomes. Camus: Sisyphus happy. Arendt: the banality of evil.
« L'existence précède l'essence », résum: "Existence precedes essence", Sartre summed up in 1946 in Existentialism is a Humanism: humans have no nature fixed in advance, they define themselves by their acts and bear the responsibility. In 1949 Simone de Beauvoir wrote in The Second Sex: "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." Sartre would refuse the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1964, so as not to be turned into an institution.
Camus, lui, part de l'absurde : le monde: Camus started from the absurd: the world does not answer our need for meaning. The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) ends: one must imagine Sisyphus happy. And in 1963 Hannah Arendt, sent to the Eichmann trial, spoke of the "banality of evil": the man who organised the deportations was not a monster but an ordinary bureaucrat who did not think.
Utilitarisme : le plus de bien-être tota: Utilitarianism: the most total well-being (Bentham, Mill). Singer: the pond (1972). Nozick: the experience machine (1974).
Pour l'utilitarisme de Jeremy Bentham, p: For the utilitarianism of Jeremy Bentham, then John Stuart Mill, the right action is the one that produces the most total well-being, for everyone it affects. Acts are judged by their consequences. Bentham even had his body preserved, still on display at University College London. Careful: utilitarianism does not say "the end justifies the means", it counts the means among the consequences too.
En 1972, Peter Singer pousse la logique: In 1972 Peter Singer pushed the logic: you would save a child drowning in a pond at the cost of your shoes; why not a child on the other side of the world, for the same price? In 1975 he also popularised the word "speciesism", proposed by Richard Ryder in 1970. Robert Nozick objected in 1974 with his experience machine: would you plug your brain into a simulated perfect life? Most people refuse.
Ce qu'on ne fait pas, quoi qu'il arrive: What you do not do, whatever happens
Kant (1785) : agir selon une maxime univ: Kant (1785): act on a maxim that can be universalised. Some acts are forbidden, whatever the consequences.
Kant répond autrement. En 1785, dans les: Kant answered differently. In 1785, in the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, he formulated the categorical imperative: act only according to the maxim that you can will to become a universal law. If everyone lied whenever it suited them, words would be worth nothing, and lying itself would become impossible.
Kant va jusqu'au bout : en 1797, réponda: Kant went all the way: in 1797, replying to Benjamin Constant, he argued that it is forbidden to lie even to a murderer who asks where your friend is hiding. Few Kantians follow him that far. But the central idea remains: some actions are forbidden whatever the consequences, and a person must never be treated merely as a means.
Tramway (Foot, 1967) : dévier oui, pouss: Trolley (Foot, 1967): switch yes, push no, for the same toll. Virtues: you become what you practise.
En 1967, Philippa Foot pose le dilemme d: In 1967 Philippa Foot posed the trolley problem: a runaway trolley will kill five people; by switching it, it will kill only one. Do you do it? Most say yes. Judith Jarvis Thomson then invented variants, including the footbridge: pushing a man onto the track to stop the trolley. Same toll, one life for five, and yet almost everyone refuses. Our intuitions are not purely utilitarian.
En 2018, l'expérience Moral Machine du M: In 2018 MIT's Moral Machine experiment gathered nearly 40 million decisions in 233 countries and territories on self-driving car dilemmas; preferences vary across cultures. Virtue ethics, inherited from Aristotle, shifts the question: not "what should I do?" but "what person should I become?". You become brave by doing brave acts, as you become a lyre player by playing the lyre.
Hobbes (1651) : la sécurité contre la li: Hobbes (1651): security in exchange for liberty. Locke: protecting natural rights. Rousseau (1762): the general will.
Pour Thomas Hobbes, dans le Léviathan (1: For Thomas Hobbes, in Leviathan (1651), without a State there is a war of every man against every man, and life would be "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short". To escape it, everyone hands their liberty to an all-powerful sovereign. For John Locke, on the contrary, power exists only to protect natural rights, life, liberty, property; a tyrannical power may be overthrown.
Rousseau, en 1762, veut que le peuple so: Rousseau, in 1762, wanted the sovereign people to obey only the laws it had given itself: law expresses the general will. Much earlier, Plato entrusted the ideal city to philosopher-kings, wary of the democracy that had condemned Socrates. And Aristotle saw man as a political animal: whoever lives outside the city is "either a beast or a god".
Montesquieu (1748) : législatif, exécuti: Montesquieu (1748): separate legislature, executive, judiciary. Mill (1859): liberty is limited only to prevent harm to others.
En 1748, dans De l'esprit des lois, Mont: In 1748, in The Spirit of the Laws, Montesquieu wrote: "To prevent the abuse of power, things must be so arranged that power checks power." Hence the separation of the legislature, which makes laws, from the executive, which applies them, and the judiciary, which judges. He did not start from nothing: he drew on Locke and on what he observed in England.
Even in a democracy the danger remains. Tocqueville, in Democracy in America, feared the tyranny of the majority, which can oppress as surely as a king, and more discreetly. John Stuart Mill replied in 1859 with On Liberty: the only legitimate reason to limit someone's liberty is to prevent harm to others. Over himself, the individual is sovereign.
Rawls (1971) : choisir sous un voile d'i: Rawls (1971): choosing behind a veil of ignorance. Weber (1919): monopoly of legitimate violence. Popper: paradox of tolerance.
En 1971, dans Théorie de la justice, Joh: In 1971, in A Theory of Justice, John Rawls proposed an experiment: choose a society's rules behind a veil of ignorance, without knowing what place you will have in it. You might be born poor, ill or in a minority. Rawls thought you would then choose equal liberties for all, and accept inequalities only if they also benefit the worst off.
D'autres pensent l'État par la force ou: Others think of the State in terms of force or resistance. For Max Weber, in 1919, the State is what successfully claims the monopoly of legitimate physical violence. Henry David Thoreau, jailed for a night in 1846 for refusing to pay tax, theorised civil disobedience, which Gandhi and Martin Luther King would read. And Karl Popper, in 1945, stated the paradox of tolerance: unlimited tolerance towards the intolerant ends up destroying tolerance.
Descartes : deux substances, reliées par: Descartes: two substances, linked by the pineal gland. Ryle (1949): the "ghost in the machine". Functionalism: the mind is what it does.
Pour Descartes, l'esprit, res cogitans,: For Descartes the mind, res cogitans, and the body, res extensa, are two different substances. It remains to explain how they communicate. He proposed the pineal gland, chosen because it is single at the centre of the brain rather than paired. We now know that it mainly secretes melatonin, the sleep hormone.
En 1949, dans La Notion d'esprit, Gilber: In 1949, in The Concept of Mind, Gilbert Ryle mocked this dualism: he called it the "ghost in the machine", a philosopher's myth. For materialism, the mind is what the brain does. For functionalism, it is defined by what it does, not by what it is made of: a well-organised machine could then have a mind. Alyca follows the debate with interest.
Turing (1950) : le jeu de l'imitation. S: Turing (1950): the imitation game. Searle (1980): the Chinese room, rules without understanding.
En 1950, dans Computing Machinery and In: In 1950, in Computing Machinery and Intelligence, Alan Turing replaced the question "can a machine think?" with a game: the imitation game. A judge converses in writing with a human and a machine; if they cannot tell them apart, by what right deny the machine the word "think"?
En 1980, John Searle répond avec la cham: In 1980 John Searle replied with the Chinese room. A man shut in a room receives questions in Chinese and, using a rule book, sends back perfect answers without understanding a word. Manipulating symbols according to rules would therefore not be enough to understand. Passing the Turing test would not prove consciousness. Alyca finds the example a little personal.
Nagel (1974) : la chauve-souris. Jackson: Nagel (1974): the bat. Jackson (1982): Mary. Chalmers (1995): the hard problem. Libet (1983): hotly debated.
En 1974, Thomas Nagel demande : quel eff: In 1974 Thomas Nagel asked: what is it like to be a bat? You can know everything about echolocation without knowing what it is like to live it. These subjective feelings, the red of your red, are called qualia. In 1982 Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a scientist who knows everything about colour but has lived in a black and white room: the day she sees a tomato, does she learn something?
En 1995, David Chalmers sépare les probl: In 1995 David Chalmers separated the "easy" problems of consciousness, explaining attention or perception, from the "hard problem": why is all this accompanied by feeling? And in 1983 Benjamin Libet measured brain activity, the readiness potential, that precedes the felt decision to move by about a third of a second. Its interpretation regarding free will remains hotly debated.
Induction : des milliers d'observations: Induction: thousands of observations do not prove the next one (Hume, Russell's chicken). Observation depends on what you know.
Une dinde est nourrie chaque matin à 9 h: A turkey is fed every morning at 9 o'clock. Day after day it concludes that it always will be. It has its throat cut on Christmas Eve. This is the popular version of an example by Bertrand Russell, who spoke of a chicken, in 1912 in The Problems of Philosophy. It illustrates Hume's problem of induction: no accumulation of observations logically guarantees the next one.
Dans les années 1920 et 1930, le cercle: In the 1920s and 1930s the Vienna Circle, with Carnap, Schlick and Neurath, wanted a science based on experience and judged metaphysics meaningless, neither true nor false. Popper countered with falsifiability. And Norwood Russell Hanson pointed out in 1958 that observation is not neutral: do Tycho Brahe and Kepler, watching the sunrise, see the same thing?
Duhem-Quine : on teste un réseau, pas un: Duhem-Quine: you test a web, not a lone hypothesis. Neptune (1846): a successful rescue. Vulcan: the theory had to change.
La thèse de Duhem-Quine dit qu'on ne tes: The Duhem-Quine thesis says you never test a hypothesis alone, but together with a whole web of auxiliary hypotheses: if the experiment fails, the fault may lie with the hypothesis, the instrument or a side theory. Which to sacrifice? In 1846 Uranus was not following its predicted orbit. Rather than throw out Newton's mechanics, Le Verrier assumed an unknown planet. Johann Galle found it less than a degree from the predicted position: Neptune.
Le Verrier recommence pour expliquer les: Le Verrier tried again to explain Mercury's anomalies and predicted Vulcan. It did not exist: general relativity was needed. Imre Lakatos drew a rule from this: a research programme is "progressive" when it predicts unexpected things that turn out true, and "degenerates" when it only patches up its failures after the fact.
Reproductibilité : environ 36 % sur 100: Replication: about 36 % of 100 studies (2015). Sokal (1996): the hoax. Preregister, replicate.
En 2015, l'Open Science Collaboration te: In 2015 the Open Science Collaboration tried to reproduce 100 psychology studies published in good journals. It found a significant result for only about 36 % of them. That is not necessarily fraud: often an effect too weak, a sample too small, or analyses chosen after seeing the data. The replication crisis has pushed researchers to preregister studies.
La relecture a ses failles. En 1996, le: Peer review has its flaws. In 1996 the physicist Alan Sokal got the journal Social Text to publish a hoax arguing that quantum gravity is a social construct; no physicist had reviewed it. Paul Feyerabend provoked in 1975 with Against Method: no rule was respected by all the great discoverers. Scientific realism replies with Putnam's no-miracles argument: if our theories were not roughly true, their success would be a miracle.
